Voici un protocole pratique (à adapter au score de Child-Pugh, à la fonction rénale, à l’âge et à la comédication). Information générale à valider selon vos protocoles locaux.

1) Évaluation initiale (avant tout ajustement)
- Déterminer: dose totale de morphine sur 24 h (incluant les prises “de secours”), voie d’administration, douleur (EVA), sédation, FR, état neuro (risque d’encéphalopathie), constipation, nausées.
- Bilan: Child-Pugh, créatinine/DFG, interactions (benzodiazépines, alcool, gabapentinoïdes).
- Privilégier formes à libération immédiate au départ; éviter la LP tant que la dose n’est pas stabilisée.

2) Principes en insuffisance hépatique avancée
- Diminuer la dose initiale et allonger les intervalles: start low, go slow.
- Éviter les hausses rapides; attendre 24 h (IR) à 48–72 h (LP) entre ajustements.
- Surveiller de près la sédation et la FR; la demi-vie peut être prolongée.

3) Si le patient est déjà sous morphine (dose jugée trop élevée)
- Calculer la dose totale des dernières 24 h.
- Réduire la dose quotidienne:
  • IH modérée: −30 à −50%
  • IH sévère (Child-Pugh C): −50 à −75% et/ou allonger l’intervalle
- Redistribuer en prises IR:
  • Exemple: si 60 mg/j PO entraînent une sédation, passer à 20–30 mg/j, soit 5 mg PO toutes les 8 h (ou 2,5–5 mg q6–8h selon tolérance).
- Dose de secours: 5% de la nouvelle dose quotidienne (plutôt que 10%), à intervalle espacé (q6–8 h PRN), avec réévaluation si >3–4 prises/j.

4) Si patient « opioid-naïf »
- PO libération immédiate: 1–2,5 mg q6–8 h. Titrer par paliers de 1–2,5 mg, augmentation de 25–33%/24 h si douleur insuffisamment contrôlée sans sédation.
- SC/IV (si voie orale aléatoire ou ascite majeure):
  • Bolus 0,5–1 mg SC/IV q4–6 h PRN, ou
  • Perfusion continue initiale 0,2–0,5 mg/h avec bolus 0,2–0,5 mg q30–60 min PRN.
- Toujours instaurer un laxatif de fond (p. ex. macrogol/senna) et un antiémétique au besoin.

5) Titration et passage à LP (si nécessaire)
- Réévaluer q4–6 h au début (IR): douleur, sédation, FR, confusion.
- Augmenter de 25–50% la dose quotidienne si EVA >4 sans signes de surdosage.
- En cas d’effets indésirables (somnolence, confusion, FR <10/min): espacer les prises et/ou réduire de 25–50%; envisager une dose sautée.
- Quand analgésie stable 48–72 h: convertir en forme LP à 50–67% de la dose quotidienne totale réellement utilisée en IH sévère; conserver l’IR pour les accès douloureux (5% TDD).

6) Surveillance et sécurité
- Paramètres: sédation (échelle simple), FR, SaO2 si dispo, état cognitif/asterixis, transit.
- Prévenir/limiter co-sédatifs (benzodiazépines, antihistaminiques sédatifs, alcool).
- Si signes de toxicité opioïde (somnolence non éveillable, FR <8/min, myoclonies, hallucinations): suspendre les doses, oxygène, envisager naloxone titrée à petites doses selon protocole, rechercher facteurs favorisants (IR, interactions, déshydratation).

7) Quand envisager une alternative
- Si toxicité récurrente malgré faibles doses ou encéphalopathie fluctuante: envisager rotation opioïde.
  • Hydromorphone IR: démarrer à ~25–50% des doses d’équianalgésie usuelles; ex. 0,5–1 mg PO q6–8 h, titration prudente.
  • Fentanyl IV/SC (en milieu monitoré) peut être utile; la forme transdermique seulement après stabilisation et besoin opioïde constant.
- Adapter à la fonction rénale (accumulation des glucuronides si DFG bas).

Points clés à préciser pour un schéma chiffré plus ciblé:
- Dose/voie actuelles de morphine, nombre de prises PRN, EVA et sédation
- Child-Pugh, DFG, poids/âge, co-médications sédatives
- Voie prévue (PO vs SC/IV)

Here’s a quick guide to what “normal” menstrual changes can look like, and when to check in with a clinician.

What’s typically normal
- Cycle length: Adults ~21–35 days; teens (first 2–3 years after first period) ~21–45 days.
- Period length: About 2–7 days.
- Flow: Can vary cycle to cycle. It’s common to be heaviest in the first 1–2 days, then lighten. Total loss is hard to measure, but not soaking a pad/tampon more than every 2 hours is a rough sign of normal.
- Color: Bright red to dark brown is common; brown/“rusty” blood at the beginning or end is just older blood.
- Clots: Small clots (dime to quarter size) occasionally can be normal.
- Cramps: Mild to moderate cramps, back ache, and bloating that improve with heat or over‑the‑counter pain relievers are common.
- PMS: Mild mood changes, breast tenderness, headaches, and fatigue in the week before a period are common.
- Mid‑cycle changes: Clear stretchy cervical mucus around ovulation and brief, mild ovulation cramps (mittelschmerz) can be normal.
- Cycle-to-cycle variation: A shift of a few days earlier or later is common, especially with stress, travel, illness, or big changes in exercise or weight.

Normal changes across life stages or situations
- First few years after menarche: Irregular timing and variable flow are common as the cycle matures.
- Hormonal birth control: 
  - Pills/patch/ring/implant: Irregular spotting is common for the first 3–6 months; periods often become lighter or may stop.
  - Hormonal IUD: Irregular spotting at first, then lighter periods or none at all.
  - Copper IUD: Periods may become heavier and crampier, especially in the first months.
- After stopping hormonal contraception: Cycles may be irregular for 1–3 months while ovulation resumes.
- Postpartum and breastfeeding: Periods may be absent or irregular for months; the first cycles can be heavier or crampier.
- Perimenopause (often mid‑ to late‑40s): Cycles may shorten, then become irregular with skipped periods; flow can be lighter or heavier. Hot flashes, sleep or mood changes may appear. Menopause = 12 months without a period.
- Lifestyle/medical factors: Stress, major weight change, very intense exercise, travel, thyroid issues, and some medicines (e.g., anticoagulants) can alter cycles.

When to seek medical advice
- Soaking through a pad/tampon every hour for 2+ hours, passing large clots repeatedly, or bleeding >7–8 days.
- Periods consistently <21 days apart or >35 days apart (adults), or a change where cycles vary by more than about a week from month to month.
- No period for >3 months (and not pregnant, postpartum, or on methods that commonly stop periods).
- Severe pain that doesn’t improve with NSAIDs/heat or that limits activities.
- Frequent bleeding between periods or after sex.
- New or concerning changes after age 45, or any bleeding after menopause.
- Signs of anemia (fatigue, shortness of breath, dizziness, pale skin).
- Positive pregnancy test or period is late with pregnancy symptoms.
- Very heavy bleeding at first period or a history suggesting a bleeding disorder.

Self-care tips
- Track cycles and symptoms (app or calendar) to spot your normal pattern.
- For cramps/heavy flow: NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen at the onset can reduce pain and flow (avoid if you have ulcers, kidney disease, or are on blood thinners; take with food).
- Heat, light exercise, hydration, and sleep help.
- If flow is heavy, consider an iron‑rich diet or ask about iron testing.

If you’d like, tell me your age, contraception (if any), pregnancy possibility, and what change you’ve noticed (timing, flow, pain, spotting). I can help sort out whether it sounds within normal range and what to do next.

Short answer: Don’t give antivenom just because it was a snake bite. Give it if there’s evidence of envenomation or clear progression. Call your regional poison center/toxicologist now for product choice and dosing.

Immediate steps
- ABCs. IV access, cardiac/SpO2 monitoring. Keep the patient at rest; immobilize the bitten limb in a functional position at heart level. Remove rings/watches.
- No incision, suction, tourniquets, or ice. Do not apply pressure immobilization if you suspect a viper/pit viper (significant local swelling/necrosis). Pressure immobilization is useful for neurotoxic elapids/sea snakes (Australia/SEA) when there is minimal swelling.
- Clean wound; update tetanus. Avoid IM injections. Provide analgesia (opioids/acetaminophen; avoid NSAIDs if coagulopathy is possible).

Assess for envenomation (treat based on syndrome, not snake ID)
- Local cytotoxic/viper syndrome: progressive pain/swelling/ecchymosis, blistering; labs: thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT/INR, low fibrinogen, elevated D‑dimer.
- Neurotoxic elapid syndrome: ptosis, dysarthria/dysphagia, paresthesias, bulbar weakness, respiratory compromise; minimal local findings.
- Myotoxic (sea snake/Some Australian elapids): severe myalgia, dark urine, rising CK, hyperkalemia.
- Systemic toxicity: vomiting, hypotension/shock, bleeding, hematuria, AKI.
- If resources are limited, 20‑minute whole blood clotting test (clean, dry glass tube): failure to clot suggests viper-induced coagulopathy.

Baseline and serial monitoring
- Mark and time the leading edge of swelling; reassess q15–30 min initially.
- Labs now and q4–6 h: CBC, PT/INR, fibrinogen, D‑dimer, CMP, CK, UA (heme/myoglobin). Consider VBG/ABG if respiratory concern.

Indications to start antivenom now
- Any systemic signs (neurotoxicity, hypotension/shock, vomiting refractory to PO/IV meds, bleeding).
- Coagulopathy/hematologic toxicity (abnormal 20WBCT, rising PT/INR, low fibrinogen, thrombocytopenia) or clinically significant bleeding.
- Rapidly progressive/local tissue effects (swelling crossing a major joint or progressing >2–3 cm per hour, severe pain, bullae/necrosis).
- Myotoxicity (rising CK, myoglobinuria, hyperkalemia).
Notes:
- Dose is not weight based; it’s based on severity.
- Have anaphylaxis supplies ready; premedication is not routinely required. Treat reactions with epinephrine IM, fluids, antihistamines, steroids as needed.

If no clear envenomation
- Observe closely (adults and kids) with serial exams and labs.
- Duration: at least 8–12 hours for viper/pit viper risk; up to 24 hours if neurotoxic elapid (e.g., coral/krait) is possible because symptoms can be delayed.
- Discharge only if exam and labs remain normal and swelling is non-progressive.

Regional product guidance (confirm locally)
- United States (pit vipers): CroFab initial 4–6 vials IV; repeat until “control” (halted swelling, improved labs/systemic signs), then 2 vials q6h ×3. OR Anavip initial 10 vials; repeat 10 if no control after ~1 h; maintenance usually not needed. Coral snake antivenom is limited—consult poison control.
- India/SE Asia/Africa: Use regionally available polyvalent antivenom for neurotoxic or hemotoxic syndromes. Typical initial 8–10 vials (may need more) for significant systemic or progressive local effects; repeat per response and 20WBCT/labs.
- Australia/PNG: Pressure immobilization early if minimal swelling; give type-specific or polyvalent antivenom for systemic signs or abnormal labs; dosing per local guidelines/toxicologist.

Additional points
- Avoid prophylactic antibiotics; treat only if infection is suspected later.
- Do not give blood products for coagulopathy unless life-threatening bleeding or after antivenom if coagulopathy persists.
- Compartment syndrome is rare; do not fasciotomize before antivenom and objective pressure measurements.
- Antivenom adverse effects: anaphylaxis (immediate) and serum sickness (5–14 days; fever, rash, arthralgias—treat with antihistamines +/- steroids).

Contact help
- US: Poison Control 1-800-222-1222 (they can connect you to a medical toxicologist).
- Australia: Poisons Information Centre 13 11 26.
- Elsewhere: your national/regional poison centre or on-call toxicologist.

Quick questions to tailor advice
- Where are you located (country/region)? Time since bite? Adult/child?
- Current symptoms and exam: pain/swelling progression, neuro signs, vitals, airway?
- Initial labs (PT/INR, fibrinogen, platelets, CK, creatinine, UA)?
- Any pressure bandage in place now?

If you share these, I can help decide whether to start antivenom and suggest product/dosing specific to your region.

Vaginal dryness is very common after childbirth, especially if you’re breastfeeding. Estrogen levels drop, which can make the vaginal tissue drier and more sensitive. The good news: simple lubricants and moisturizers usually help a lot.

Quick choices
- For sex right now (lubricants):
  - Water‑based: gentle, easy to clean, safe with condoms. Examples: Sliquid H2O, Good Clean Love Almost Naked, YES WB. If you get yeast infections, choose glycerin‑free (like Sliquid H2O or YES WB).
  - Silicone‑based: very long‑lasting, great if water‑based dries too fast; also safe with latex condoms. Examples: Uberlube, Pjur Original. Avoid with silicone sex toys (can damage them).
  - Avoid oil‑based lubes (coconut oil, petroleum jelly) if you use latex condoms or are prone to irritation/UTIs. Oils can weaken latex and disrupt the vaginal microbiome.

  - Use 2–3 times per week. Options: hyaluronic acid or polycarbophil products such as Revaree (HA), YES VM, or Replens. These can reduce daily dryness and make sex more comfortable over time.

How to use
- Apply a generous amount of lube to you and your partner/sex toy before penetration; reapply as needed.

I’m sorry this is worrying you. Hand shaking and feeling clumsy can have many causes, and Huntington’s disease (HD) is only one—and is unlikely in most 29-year-olds, especially without a family history.

A few points that may help:
- What HD typically looks like: it usually starts between 30–50 with involuntary, dance-like jerking (chorea) rather than a pure tremor, plus changes in mood/behavior and thinking over time. It’s autosomal dominant—most people who develop it have a parent with HD. New (de novo) cases are rare.
- Common non-HD causes of tremor/clumsiness at your age: anxiety/stress, too much caffeine or stimulants (including decongestants, energy drinks, ADHD meds), alcohol withdrawal, thyroid overactivity, low blood sugar, vitamin B12 deficiency, medication side effects (SSRIs/SNRIs, lithium, valproate, antipsychotics, albuterol), essential tremor, migraine, and less commonly neurological conditions like Wilson’s disease (a treatable copper metabolism disorder), dystonia, or multiple sclerosis.

Questions that help narrow it down:
- Do you have a family history of HD or relatives with early-onset movement problems, psychiatric changes, or early dementia?
- Is the shaking at rest or mainly when you hold something or reach for things? Does stress, caffeine, or fatigue make it worse? Does a small amount of alcohol reduce it?
- Any other symptoms: mood or behavior changes, cognitive difficulties, weight loss, trouble with eye movements, slurred speech, balance problems, weakness, numbness, vision changes, or new headaches?
- What meds/supplements or substances do you use (including caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, stimulants, inhalers)?
- Any recent illness, sleep loss, or increased stress?

What to do next:
- See your primary care clinician for a focused neurologic exam and basic labs: thyroid (TSH), metabolic panel, glucose, CBC, vitamin B12. Given your age, ask about screening for Wilson’s disease (ceruloplasmin, serum/urine copper) if symptoms persist or exam is abnormal.
- If symptoms are progressive, impact daily life, or your exam is abnormal, ask for a neurology referral. If there is a strong family history of HD or your neurologic exam suggests it, testing is usually arranged through a neurologist/genetic counselor (not via direct-to-consumer kits), because genetic testing has important counseling considerations.
- In the meantime: cut back on caffeine/energy drinks, review meds with your doctor, sleep well, stay hydrated, manage stress/anxiety. If the tremor interferes with tasks, your doctor can discuss treatments for essential tremor (for example, propranolol or primidone) if appropriate.

Urgent care now if you develop any red flags: sudden severe headache, new weakness or numbness on one side, facial droop, trouble speaking, severe balance problems or repeated falls, double vision, or rapidly worsening symptoms.

Short answer: nobody can give a firm date, and “completely safe” is unlikely for any transplant. But if early trials continue to go well, pig-to-human (xenotransplant) kidneys could move from rare, highly controlled cases to limited routine use in specialized centers in the early–to–mid 2030s. Hearts will likely lag several years; livers and lungs are farther out and may take decades, if they become routine at all.

Where things stand (late 2024 knowledge):
- Multiple short-term successes in brain-dead models; two pig hearts transplanted into living patients survived weeks; the first living recipient of a pig kidney was transplanted in 2024 and initially did well. No product is FDA-approved; use has been under single-patient emergency/compassionate pathways and very early trials.
- Key risks remain: immune rejection (especially chronic), clotting/inflammation, organ growth and function mismatches, and infection control (e.g., porcine cytomegalovirus; porcine endogenous retroviruses are being engineered out and haven’t been seen to transmit to humans so far).

What “routine” would require:
- Reproducible 1–3 year graft survival and function across multiple centers, approaching human donor outcomes (for kidneys, ≥85–90% 1‑year survival and acceptable safety).
- Clear infectious-disease safety with pathogen-free herds and long-term recipient monitoring frameworks.
- Standardized immunosuppression that’s effective and tolerable.
- Scalable, regulated animal production and logistics; payer coverage and clinician training.

Plausible timelines (best-case, evidence-based estimates):
- Kidneys: most likely first. If Phase 1/2 data over the next 3–5 years show durable function and safety, conditional or limited approvals in specialized centers could begin early–mid 2030s. Broader availability would follow as longer-term data accrue.
- Hearts: additional hurdles (hemodynamics, thrombosis, rejection). If progress continues, limited use for select patients could emerge mid–to–late 2030s; “routine” use would likely be later.
- Livers and lungs: technically the hardest (coagulation and lung injury issues). These may remain bridges to human transplant for a long time; routine use, if it comes, is more likely in the 2040s or beyond.
- Islet cells and some tissues (e.g., skin, corneas, valves): may reach routine use sooner than whole-organ solid organ xenotransplants in specific indications.

Bottom line: Expect a gradual, stepwise rollout—first in tightly controlled trials and a few expert centers, then expanding if outcomes match or beat current standards. If you’re thinking about a specific organ or condition, I can give a more tailored outlook.

Siento que estés pasando por esto. La buena noticia es que hoy el VIH se trata con una pastilla al día, es muy eficaz y, con adherencia, podrás tener una vida larga y plena. Además, al lograr una carga viral indetectable, no transmites el virus por vía sexual (U=U).

Qué hacer ahora (primeras semanas)
- Agenda cita con un especialista en VIH/enfermedades infecciosas lo antes posible. En muchos lugares pueden iniciar tratamiento el mismo día.
- Exámenes iniciales: carga viral, CD4, función renal y hepática, hemograma, perfil lipídico y glucosa, genotipo de resistencia, serologías de hepatitis B y C, prueba de TB, sífilis y otras ITS; en mujeres con potencial de embarazo, prueba de embarazo. Considerar HLA‑B*57:01 si se evalúa abacavir.
- Vacunas: hepatitis A/B (si no inmune), influenza anual, COVID‑19, neumococo, tétanos/difteria/pertussis, VPH; sarampión/varicela solo si CD4 >200 y no inmune.

Tratamiento inicial recomendado
La terapia antirretroviral (TAR) estándar combina 2 análogos de nucleósidos + un inhibidor de integrasa. Opciones de primera línea usadas en 2024/25:

1) Bictegravir/tenofovir alafenamida/emtricitabina (BIC/TAF/FTC) – 1 tableta diaria.
- Pros: muy potente, bien tolerada, activa contra hepatitis B, se puede iniciar antes de tener el genotipo.
- Consideraciones: preferir si función renal eGFR ≥30 ml/min; vigilar peso y lípidos.

2) Dolutegravir + tenofovir (TAF o TDF) + emtricitabina (FTC) o lamivudina (3TC) – 1–2 tabletas diarias.
- Pros: también de primera línea global, seguro en embarazo y para inicio rápido.
- TAF se prefiere si hay riesgo óseo/renal; TDF puede ser preferible si hay riesgo cardiovascular elevado.

3) Dolutegravir/lamivudina (DTG/3TC)
- Úsalo solo si: carga viral <500,000 copias/ml, sin coinfección por hepatitis B, y genotipo sin resistencia. No es ideal para “inicio el mismo día” si aún no tienes estos datos.

Alternativas en casos especiales
- Darunavir potenciado + TAF/FTC o TDF/FTC (p. ej., Symtuza) cuando hay alta sospecha de resistencia o interacciones; más efectos adversos metabólicos.
- Evitar iniciar abacavir sin prueba HLA‑B*57:01 y si hay riesgo cardiovascular alto.
- Cabotegravir/rilpivirina inyectable es para mantenimiento una vez indetectable, no para empezar.

Si hay coinfección por hepatitis B
- El esquema debe incluir TAF o TDF junto con FTC o 3TC de manera continua (BIC/TAF/FTC o DTG + TAF/TDF + FTC/3TC).

Efectos secundarios comunes
- En general leves: náuseas, dolor de cabeza, sueño vívido o insomnio los primeros días-semanas. Suele mejorar.
- Posible aumento de peso con inhibidores de integrasa.
- Avísale a tu médico si notas sarpullido, ictericia, dolor intenso o síntomas nuevos.

Prevención y pareja(s)
- U=U: al estar indetectable de forma sostenida no transmites el VIH por sexo.
- Recomienda a tu(s) pareja(s) hacerse pruebas; si hubo exposición reciente, considerar PEP/PrEP.
- Usa condón hasta que estés indetectable y para prevenir otras ITS.

Profilaxis de infecciones oportunistas
- Si CD4 <200, puede indicarse trimetoprim-sulfametoxazol (cotrimoxazol) hasta recuperación de CD4.
- Tu equipo definirá si necesitas otras profilaxis según CD4 y antecedentes.

Seguimiento
- Control y exámenes a las 2–4 semanas de iniciar TAR, luego cada 1–3 meses hasta indetectable, y después cada 3–6 meses.
- Adherencia diaria es clave; configura recordatorios.

Cómo conseguir los medicamentos
- Varía por país. En muchos lugares, la TAR es gratuita a través del sistema público:
  - España: hospitales públicos y farmacia hospitalaria.
  - México: CAPASITS/SAIIC y unidades de la Secretaría de Salud/IMSS/ISSSTE.
  - Argentina: Programa Nacional de VIH; hospitales públicos/obras sociales.
  - Chile: garantizado por GES/AUGE en el sistema público.
  - Colombia: EPS a través de su red de infectología.
  - Perú: MINSA/ESSALUD en hospitales de referencia.
  - Estados Unidos: clínicas Ryan White/ADAP; también seguros privados/Medicaid/Medicare.
- Si me dices en qué país/ciudad estás, te indico rutas y contactos específicos.

Para personalizar la mejor opción para ti, cuéntame:
- Tu país/ciudad y si ya tienes cita con infectología.
- Resultados de CD4, carga viral y si te han hecho genotipo.
- Si tienes enfermedad renal/ósea, factores de riesgo cardiovascular, embarazo o planes de embarazo, o hepatitis B/C.
- Medicamentos actuales o suplementos.

No estás solo. Además del equipo médico, hay ONGs y grupos de apoyo que pueden ayudarte con información, emociones y trámites. Si te sientes abrumado o con angustia intensa, dímelo y busquemos apoyo inmediato.

Short answer
- Evidence for cannabis-based topicals (creams, balms, gels) in painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy is preliminary. A few small, short-duration randomized trials in peripheral neuropathy suggest modest benefit, but there are no large, high‑quality, long‑term studies confirming efficacy or safety.
- Short-term safety of CBD-dominant topicals looks acceptable in trials (mostly mild local skin reactions, no serious systemic events), but long‑term safety over months to years hasn’t been established.
- Current neuropathic pain guidelines do not recommend topical cannabinoids because of insufficient evidence. If patients wish to try them, use as an adjunct with careful product selection and monitoring.

What’s known from studies
- One small randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial (about 4 weeks, ~30 participants) found that a CBD topical reduced neuropathic pain symptoms (intense/sharp/cold/itchy sensations) versus placebo in mixed peripheral neuropathy; no significant adverse events were reported. Duration was short and sample size small, so certainty is low.
- A handful of small open-label studies and case series in peripheral neuropathic pain report benefit signals with topical CBD, but designs are at high risk of bias.
- Systematic reviews through 2023–2024 conclude: very low to low certainty evidence; heterogenous products/doses; short follow‑up; no robust data for diabetic neuropathy specifically; safety appears acceptable short term, long‑term unknown.
- Transdermal (designed for systemic absorption) cannabinoid gels/patches are a different category; some have shown mixed or negative results for other pain conditions and can produce systemic exposures and drug interactions.

Safety considerations
- Local: irritant or allergic contact dermatitis (often due to fragrances/terpenes/menthols, not CBD itself); folliculitis with occlusive products. Patch‑test on a small area first; avoid broken skin/ulcers.
- Systemic: with true creams/balms intended for local effect, systemic absorption of CBD is usually minimal; psychoactive effects from THC are unlikely unless the product contains appreciable THC or is transdermal. However, mislabeling is common.
- Product quality: independent testing frequently finds inaccurate CBD content, unexpected THC, pesticides/solvents/heavy metals, and undisclosed additives. This is a major practical risk.
- Drug testing: even “THC-free” products have occasionally contained THC; a positive drug test is possible if contaminated.
- Special populations: avoid in pregnancy/breastfeeding; use extra caution with anticoagulants or narrow-therapeutic-index drugs if there’s any chance of systemic absorption (especially with transdermals).

How to counsel patients who want to try a topical
- Set expectations: Evidence is preliminary; consider a time‑limited trial as an adjunct to guideline‑based therapy. If no meaningful benefit (e.g., ≥30% pain reduction or function/sleep improvement) after 4–8 weeks, stop.
- Choose safer products:
  - Prefer CBD‑dominant topicals (not transdermals) from manufacturers providing a recent third‑party certificate of analysis (COA) that matches the batch, shows CBD amount, non-detectable THC (or ≤0.3% if hemp-derived), and tests for heavy metals, pesticides, microbes, and residual solvents.
  - Avoid products with multiple fragrances/essential oils or menthol/camphor if the patient has sensitive skin or eczema.
- Use: apply to intact skin; start small area once daily for 48 hours to check for irritation, then 2–3 times daily as needed. Stop if rash, worsening symptoms, or any systemic effects occur.
- Diabetic foot care: do not apply to ulcers or macerated skin; avoid occlusive dressings; inspect skin daily given reduced sensation.

Alternatives with stronger evidence for painful diabetic neuropathy
- Systemic: duloxetine or pregabalin (first‑line), gabapentin, or a TCA in selected patients; consider combination therapy when appropriate.
- Topical: capsaicin 8% in‑clinic patch has RCT support; 5% lidocaine patches can help focal allodynia.
- Nonpharmacologic: exercise, weight management, glycemic optimization, foot care, CBT/pain self‑management, and TENS.

Bottom line
- We don’t yet have robust, long‑term evidence that cannabis creams are both effective and safe for chronic daily use in diabetic neuropathy. Short‑term, small trials suggest possible benefit with CBD topicals and minimal adverse effects, but data quality and duration are limited, and product quality varies widely. If patients want to try them, treat as an adjunct with careful product selection, a defined trial period, and routine reassessment.

- Use AAP 2022 hyperbilirubinemia guideline hour-specific thresholds (35–37 6/7 and ≥38 weeks, with/without neurotoxicity risk factors) to interpret results. Until GA/risk factors are known, use the more conservative (lower) phototherapy thresholds and consider neurotoxicity risk factors present.
- If TSB is at/above phototherapy threshold, start intensive phototherapy promptly (overhead LED plus bili-blanket; maximize skin exposure; eye protection; thermoregulation). Recheck TSB 4–6 hours after initiation, then q12–24 hours depending on trajectory.
- If TSB is approaching exchange threshold or rising despite intensive phototherapy, consult NICU. For immune-mediated hemolysis (positive DAT) with rapidly rising bilirubin approaching exchange thresholds despite intensive phototherapy, consider IVIG 0.5–1 g/kg per AAP guidance.
- If below treatment threshold:
  - Optimize feeding (see below).
  - Repeat bilirubin based on proximity to threshold and clinical course (e.g., 6–12 hours if within ~2 mg/dL; 12–24 hours if further below), documenting age in hours.
- If direct (conjugated) bilirubin ≥1 mg/dL and >20% of TSB, evaluate for cholestasis (LFTs, abdominal exam, stool/urine color, consider GI consult).

Hemolysis assessment
- Infant blood type/Rh and DAT; review maternal type/Rh/antibody screen.
- CBC, retic, smear. If reticulocytosis or hemolysis suspected and DAT negative, consider G6PD level and hereditary spherocytosis screen (EMA binding test/OSA if available) per hematology guidance.

Feeding, hydration, and weight
- Lactation consult today if breastfeeding. Encourage 8–12 effective feeds per 24 hours; assess latch, transfer, and maternal supply.
- Strict intake/output; document urine and stool counts.
- Daily weight; calculate % weight loss from birth (obtain birth weight).
- If evidence of suboptimal intake or excessive weight loss (>7–10%), consider temporary supplementation with expressed breast milk or formula while supporting breastfeeding; reassess bilirubin trajectory.

Monitoring and safety
- Vitals q4h while inpatient.
- Neuro checks for signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy (lethargy, hypotonia/hypertonia, high-pitched cry, poor suck, retrocollis/opisthotonos).
- Maintain normothermia and adequate hydration, especially during phototherapy.

Routine newborn care
- Verify and document: Vitamin K given at birth, erythromycin eye ointment, hepatitis B vaccine (administer if not yet given and medically appropriate).
- Verify newborn metabolic screen sent; hearing screen and critical congenital heart disease (CCHD) screen before discharge.

Parental education
- Explain jaundice, typical course, and need for bilirubin measurement.
- Phototherapy purpose and safety if initiated.
- Feeding goals: at least 8–12 feeds/day, adequate urine (≥6/day by day 4–5) and transition stools.
- Red flags to report immediately: poor feeding, decreased urine/stool, fever, increasing sleepiness/difficulty to arouse, high-pitched cry, arching, progressive jaundice extending to legs/soles, dark urine or pale/white stools.

Disposition and follow-up
- Inpatient observation pending bilirubin results and trend; begin phototherapy if indicated.
- Discharge when bilirubin is safely below treatment thresholds with a down-trending pattern, feeding is adequate, weight loss acceptable, and reliable follow-up is arranged.
- Outpatient follow-up: Pediatrician visit within 24–48 hours of discharge (earlier if bilirubin near threshold or if risk factors present) with a plan for repeat bilirubin measurement as indicated by AAP 2022 follow-up recommendations.

Nigeria continues to detect circulating vaccine‑derived poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2), and poliomyelitis classically causes sudden, asymmetric, flaccid weakness with reduced reflexes and preserved sensation.

- Urgent clinical assessment
  - Full neuro exam: distribution of weakness, tone (flaccid), deep tendon reflexes (often decreased/absent in polio), sensation (typically intact), cranial nerves, bulbar/respiratory involvement.

  - Implement standard and contact (enteric) precautions; meticulous hand hygiene. Avoid unnecessary intramuscular injections or procedures during the acute phase.

  - Admit or arrange close observation if progression, pain, bulbar or respiratory signs, or diagnostic uncertainty.

What’s normal after a bug bite
- Mild redness and warmth around the bite, some swelling, itch, and a dull ache or throbbing are common.
- Symptoms usually peak in the first 24–48 hours, then slowly improve over the next few days.

Signs it may be infected (seek care)
- Redness that keeps spreading after day 2, or an area larger than about 2 inches (5 cm) and growing.
- Increasing pain (more than itch), marked tenderness, or the skin feels very hot.
- Pus, a soft spot or “head,” or a firm, painful lump (possible abscess).
- Fever, chills, feeling unwell, swollen “glands,” or red streaks going up a limb.
- The bite is on the face, near an eye, on the genitals, over a joint, or you have diabetes, poor circulation, or a weak immune system.

Allergic reactions (seek urgent/emergency help)
- Widespread hives, swelling of lips/tongue/face, trouble breathing, wheezing, vomiting, dizziness, or fainting — call emergency services.
- Large local reactions (big swelling around a sting) can look scary but are usually not infected; they peak at 24–48 hours and improve over 5–10 days. Seek care if swelling is severe or involves the face/neck.

Home care now
- Wash once with soap and water. Pat dry. Don’t pick or squeeze.
- Cool compress or ice (wrapped) 10–15 minutes at a time, several times daily.
- Elevate the area if it’s on a limb to reduce swelling.
- Itch relief: oral antihistamine like cetirizine or loratadine by day; diphenhydramine at night if needed (can make you drowsy). Follow package directions.
- Topical 1% hydrocortisone thin layer 1–2 times daily for itch/redness (avoid eyes or broken skin).
- Pain: acetaminophen or ibuprofen as needed (follow label; avoid ibuprofen if your doctor has told you not to take NSAIDs).
- If the skin is broken, keep it clean, cover with a light bandage, and change daily. Avoid routine antibiotic ointments if the skin isn’t open (they can cause rashes).

When to see someone
- See a clinician within 24–48 hours if redness, warmth, swelling, or pain are getting worse instead of better, or if the area is rapidly expanding.
- Go the same day/urgent care if you notice pus, fever, red streaks, severe pain, or the bite is on the face/near the eye.
- Lower threshold to be seen if you have diabetes, lymphedema, are on chemo/steroids/biologics, or have poor circulation.

Other things to know
- Tetanus: If the skin was punctured and your last tetanus shot was over 10 years ago (or over 5 years for a dirty wound), get a booster.
- Tick possibility (common after hiking): If it might have been a tick, watch for a spreading round/oval rash (often but not always “bull’s-eye”) or flu-like symptoms (fever, headache, fatigue, joint aches) in the next 3–30 days; get medical care if these occur. If a tick is still attached, remove with fine tweezers, grasping close to the skin and pulling straight out.
- Abscess warning: a tender, warm lump that may feel soft in the center can mean a pocket of infection. Don’t squeeze; see a clinician.
- Photos help: outline the edge of redness with a pen and take a picture to see if it’s spreading over time.

If you’d like, tell me:
- Where on your body the bite is, how big the red area is, and when it started.
- Whether you have fever or red streaks, or if there’s drainage.
- Your health conditions and last tetanus shot.
I can help you decide how urgent it is and tailor next steps.

- Age and sex?
- Current height and weight (and percentiles, if you have them) and how they’ve changed over time?
- Parents’ heights?

Key points about short stature
- Definition: Height below the 3rd percentile (about −2 SD) or a drop across two major percentile lines on the growth chart.
- Growth velocity matters: After age 4, kids should grow ~5–6 cm (2–2.5 in) per year pre-puberty. Slower growth is a red flag.
- Common normal variants:
  - Familial short stature: child tracks low percentiles but grows steadily; predicted adult height matches parents.
  - Constitutional delay: “late bloomer,” slow growth and delayed puberty, but normal adult height.
- Other causes to consider: nutrition issues, celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, kidney/heart disease, hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome (girls), genetic bone conditions, chronic steroid use, psychosocial stress.

When to see the pediatrician (or a pediatric endocrinologist)
- Height <3rd percentile or crossing down percentiles.
- Growth <5 cm/year after age 4.
- Puberty not started by 13 (girls) or 14 (boys).
- Disproportionate body segments, recurrent headaches/vision changes, persistent vomiting, chronic diarrhea/abdominal pain, unexplained weight loss, or fatigue.

What you can do now
- Get accurate measurements every 6–12 months and plot on a CDC/WHO growth chart.
- Calculate mid‑parental (target) height:
  - Boy: (mother’s height + father’s height + 13 cm) / 2.
  - Girl: (mother’s height + father’s height − 13 cm) / 2.
  - Expected adult height range is about ±8.5 cm around that number.
- Support growth: balanced diet with enough protein, calcium, and vitamin D; regular physical activity; 9–11 hours of sleep; treat chronic illnesses promptly. No supplement, stretch, or shoe insert can make a child taller beyond genetics; only treating underlying conditions can help.

What testing a doctor might order
- Bone age X‑ray (left hand/wrist).
- Labs: CBC, CMP, ESR/CRP, TSH/free T4, celiac screen (tTG‑IgA and total IgA), IGF‑1/IGFBP‑3; urinalysis; possibly karyotype in girls.
- Further endocrine testing or imaging if indicated.

About growth hormone
- Considered for specific conditions (GH deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic kidney disease, small for gestational age without catch‑up, SHOX deficiency, some cases of idiopathic short stature). Average adult height gain is modest (often 4–6 cm), involves daily injections, monitoring, and cost.

First, quickly assess

If any of the above are present (or symptoms are rapidly worsening), treat as anaphylaxis now
- Position: Lay the child flat with legs elevated. If vomiting or having trouble breathing, position on their side or sitting up slightly for comfort. Do not let them stand or walk.
- Epinephrine:

- The child should be observed in a medical facility for at least 4 hours after symptoms resolve (longer if severe or if multiple epinephrine doses were needed).

Here’s a quick, practical reference for acute pediatric glaucoma when you need to lower IOP emergently, plan sedation/EUA, and move to urgent surgery. Medical therapy is temporizing in children—definitive surgery is usually required.

When to treat as an emergency
- IOP clearly elevated with corneal edema, photophobia, blepharospasm, buphthalmos, Haab striae, or severe pain/tearing.
- Suspected primary congenital glaucoma or acute pupillary block.
- Optic nerve pallor/cupping or corneal clouding threatening vision.

Immediate steps (while arranging urgent ophthalmology)
- Measure IOP quickly (iCare/Tonopen), avoid corneal injury.
- Start topical meds with punctal occlusion 2–3 min to reduce systemic absorption.
- Give systemic therapy if IOP very high or cornea threatened.
- Control pain/nausea; keep the child NPO if EUA/surgery likely within hours.

Temporizing IOP-lowering regimen (pediatrics)
Topical (use what’s available; combine classes)
- Beta-blocker: timolol
  - <2 years: 0.25% 1 drop q12h; ≥2 years: 0.5% q12h
  - Avoid in asthma, heart block; monitor for bradycardia/apnea.
- Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor: dorzolamide 2% or brinzolamide 1% q8h
- Alpha-agonist: avoid brimonidine in children <2 years (generally avoid <6 years due to CNS depression). If needed for short-term rescue, some use apraclonidine 0.5% q8–12h with monitoring.
- Prostaglandin (e.g., latanoprost) 1 drop qhs: variable effect acutely; safe adjunct.
- Miotics (pilocarpine): not effective in primary congenital glaucoma; avoid until IOP <40 and only if treating pupillary block—do not rely on it.

Systemic (if IOP very high or cornea/nerve at risk)
- Acetazolamide (check renal function, sickle cell, sulfa allergy):
  - IV: 5–10 mg/kg as a stat dose
  - PO: 10–20 mg/kg/day divided q6–8h (temporizing until surgery)
  - Monitor electrolytes/acid–base; risk of metabolic acidosis in infants.
- Hyperosmotic agent (if no cardiac/renal failure, dehydration, intracranial hemorrhage):
  - Mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg IV over 30–60 min
  - Oral glycerol 1–1.5 g/kg or isosorbide 1.5–2 g/kg if IV access delayed and aspiration risk low
  - Monitor fluids/electrolytes; watch for pulmonary edema.

Supportive
- Topical steroid (e.g., prednisolone acetate 1%) q4–6h if corneal edema/inflammation.
- Cycloplegic for comfort (e.g., atropine 1% BID) in open angles; avoid if pupillary block suspected.

Definitive management (arrange urgently)
- Primary congenital glaucoma: surgery is first-line after brief medical stabilization.
  - Goniotomy if cornea clear enough for angle view.
  - Trabeculotomy ab externo if cornea cloudy.
  - Combined trabeculotomy–trabeculectomy if advanced/failed.
  - Aim to take to EUA and surgery within 24–48 hours (sooner if severe edema/IOP).
- Acute pupillary block/angle closure (rare in children; consider microspherophakia, ectopia lentis, aphakia/pseudophakia):
  - Temporize as above. Do not rely on pilocarpine.
  - Definitive: laser peripheral iridotomy (older cooperative child) or surgical iridectomy under GA. If lens-induced, plan lens surgery.

Sedation/anesthesia pearls (EUA/surgery)
- Coordinate early with pediatric anesthesia.
- Induction: propofol and sevoflurane decrease IOP; both are acceptable.
- Avoid/limit succinylcholine (transient IOP rise); use non-depolarizing agent (e.g., rocuronium) if needed.
- Ketamine can raise IOP slightly; prefer alternatives if glaucoma is the primary issue.
- Expect systemic effects from topicals (timolol/brimonidine)—continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring; use punctal occlusion with drops.
- Acetazolamide may worsen metabolic acidosis in infants; correct before prolonged GA.
- Maintain gentle ventilation and avoid venous congestion that can raise IOP.

Key pitfalls/contraindications
- Do not use brimonidine in children <2 years; caution <6 years.
- Pilocarpine is generally ineffective in primary congenital glaucoma and can worsen lens-related block.
- Avoid hyperosmotics in significant renal/cardiac failure or dehydration.
- Rule out masqueraders (e.g., congenital corneal dystrophies, megalocornea) and sinister causes (retinoblastoma) before assuming “glaucoma.”

Follow-up/monitoring
- Admit or observe closely if using systemic agents or if surgery planned.
- Recheck IOP within hours after hyperosmotic/acetazolamide treatment.
- Plan EUA for accurate IOP, corneal diameter, axial length, gonioscopy, and optic nerve evaluation.

Bottom line
- Use topical beta-blocker + topical CAI ± alpha-agonist (age-appropriate), add acetazolamide, and give IV mannitol if IOP is very high or cornea threatened.
- Proceed to EUA and definitive angle surgery (goniotomy/trabeculotomy) for primary congenital glaucoma, or iridectomy/LPI for pupillary block, urgently.

Here’s the workup commonly recommended in Guangdong/China for suspected paragonimiasis (lung fluke) after eating raw/undercooked freshwater snails or crabs. In practice, clinicians combine direct parasite detection with serology and imaging.

Who to test
- Compatible symptoms (fever, cough, chest/pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, abdominal pain) plus eosinophilia and a history of eating local freshwater snails/crabs.

First-line tests
- CBC with differential: check for peripheral eosinophilia; total IgE can support the diagnosis.
- Chest imaging:
  - Chest X-ray as a screen.
  - Chest CT if available: may show subpleural nodules/cysts, patchy consolidation, linear “migration tracts,” pleural effusion or hydropneumothorax.
- Parasitology (direct egg detection):
  - Sputum microscopy: 3 separate morning specimens on different days; direct wet mount and concentration (e.g., formalin–ether). Induced sputum improves yield.
  - Stool microscopy: 3 specimens with concentration methods. Less sensitive than sputum in pulmonary disease but still recommended.
  - Pleural fluid (if effusion present): cell count (often eosinophil‑predominant exudate), biochemistry, and microscopy for Paragonimus eggs.
- Serology (widely used in Guangdong/China):
  - Paragonimus IgG ELISA; high sensitivity in pulmonary and extrapulmonary disease.
  - If available, confirm positives or clarify equivocal results with immunoblot (Western blot) at a provincial/tertiary lab.
  - Note: possible cross‑reactivity with other trematodes (e.g., Clonorchis), so interpret with exposure and imaging.

Second-line/confirmatory procedures (if initial tests are negative but suspicion remains high)
- Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): microscopy for eggs; cytology can sometimes show ova.
- PCR assays for Paragonimus DNA on sputum/BAL/pleural fluid: available in some tertiary hospitals or reference labs (e.g., provincial CDC) and useful in pauciparasitic or early disease.
- Tissue sampling:
  - Ultrasound‑ or CT‑guided aspiration/biopsy of peripheral lung or pleural lesions if accessible and safe, for ova/histology.
- For suspected ectopic disease:
  - Brain MRI for cerebral paragonimiasis; CSF analysis (often eosinophilia) and CSF Paragonimus serology where available.
  - Abdominal ultrasound/CT for hepatic/peritoneal lesions.

Diagnostic pointers and interpretation
- Definitive diagnosis: demonstration of Paragonimus eggs or worms in sputum, BAL, stool, pleural fluid, or tissue; or positive PCR.
- Probable diagnosis in endemic areas: compatible exposure + typical imaging + eosinophilia + positive Paragonimus serology.
- Timing matters: eggs often appear in respiratory samples only after several weeks; antibodies typically detectable ~2–4 weeks after infection.
- Differentiate from TB: both can cause pleural effusion and elevated ADA; an eosinophil‑predominant effusion and positive Paragonimus serology favor paragonimiasis.

Where to get testing in Guangdong
- Large tertiary hospitals (e.g., Sun Yat‑sen University–affiliated hospitals, Nanfang Hospital) offer serology and advanced imaging; bronchoscopy and PCR may be available.
- Guangdong Provincial CDC and municipal CDC labs can provide or coordinate Paragonimus serology and reference testing.

Follow-up
- After treatment, eggs may disappear within weeks; eosinophils and symptoms typically decline. Serologic titers fall more slowly and may stay positive for months—use clinical and imaging response for follow‑up.

Short answer: it isn’t safe or appropriate to pick a specific ADHD medication without a proper evaluation. Stimulants are controlled substances with real risks, and the “right” option depends on your history, symptoms, and health. That said, here’s a quick guide so you can have an informed conversation with a clinician.

What clinicians usually start with
- Stimulants (first-line for most adults with confirmed ADHD)
  - Methylphenidate class (e.g., extended‑release methylphenidate). Often better tolerated if you have anxiety or tics.
  - Amphetamine class (e.g., lisdexamfetamine or mixed amphetamine salts ER). Slightly higher average efficacy for some; lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug with a smoother effect and lower misuse potential.
  - Long-acting versions are usually preferred for adults for all‑day coverage and fewer rebounds.
- Non-stimulants (when stimulants aren’t a good fit or there’s high misuse risk)
  - Atomoxetine: helpful with co‑occurring anxiety; not a controlled substance; takes 2–6 weeks to work.
  - Guanfacine ER or clonidine ER: can help with hyperactivity/impulsivity, sleep, or tics; may cause sedation and low blood pressure.
  - Bupropion (off‑label): can help if depression is also present; avoid with seizure or eating‑disorder history.

How clinicians choose
- Coexisting issues: anxiety, depression, tics, substance use risk, sleep problems.
- Heart health: personal/family history of heart disease, arrhythmias, fainting; baseline blood pressure/heart rate.
- Workday needs: desired duration, timing, and flexibility (long- vs short-acting).
- Side-effect tolerance: appetite loss, insomnia, increased BP/HR, irritability, anxiety.
- Practicalities: insurance coverage, cost, and your preferences.

Safety basics before starting
- Full assessment to confirm ADHD and rule out other causes (sleep deprivation, stress/anxiety/depression, thyroid issues, anemia, sleep apnea, med/substance effects).
- Review your meds/supplements and caffeine/nicotine/alcohol/cannabis use.
- Baseline vitals (BP, pulse, weight); consider ECG only if cardiac risk factors.
- Discuss pregnancy plans or breastfeeding if relevant.
- Ongoing monitoring: symptom ratings, appetite/weight, sleep, mood, BP/HR.

What to say at the appointment
- “I’m struggling to focus at work. I’ve tried sleep, exercise, and structure. Could we evaluate for ADHD? If appropriate, could we consider a long-acting stimulant like methylphenidate ER or lisdexamfetamine? I’m also open to non‑stimulants if you think they’re a better fit.”
- Bring a brief symptom history (including childhood), any school/work reports, and consider completing an adult ADHD screener (e.g., ASRS) beforehand.

Important cautions
- Don’t use someone else’s medication or buy it online—legal and safety risks are significant.
- Stimulants can worsen anxiety, insomnia, or raise blood pressure/heart rate; rare but serious mood or cardiac effects can occur.
- If there’s a history of substance use disorder, non‑stimulants or lisdexamfetamine may be safer choices—decide this with your clinician.
